A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of language-model elasticity using compression theory and fine-tuning experiments. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support matching content across the substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 Sections 3.3–3.4 report original fine-tuning experiments, including the loss comparisons in Table 1 and performance curves in Figures 3–5.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results in Section 4 and adds DPO, reversed-sentiment and extended-scale experiments in Appendix C.

M1.justification: The token-tree pruning/Huffman compression construction and core forward/inverse fine-tuning procedures are retained. DPO is introduced as a validation condition, without proposing a new alignment algorithm or architecture. The revised compression normalization changes the theory.

E1.justification: Instruction following, truthfulness, sentiment generation and safe conversation remain the evaluated coverage. The safety data changes from the PKU-SafeRLHF label to BeaverTails while retaining the same cited dataset work and corresponding results. Appendix C reuses IMDb under additional training and model configurations.

E2.justification: The forward-versus-inverse comparisons and pretrained reference models remain the comparison framework. DPO is used to test whether elasticity persists under another fine-tuning algorithm, rather than introduced as a competing method benchmark.

E3.justification: v3 reports three equal SFT partitions instead of four for Table 1, although its unchanged numbers do not establish rerunning. Appendix C adds DPO inverse fine-tuning, reversed sentiment roles, 0.1T/0.5T/1.0T pretraining checkpoints and Qwen1.5-72B, substantially extending the evaluation settings.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained model-size and pretraining-volume analyses, Appendix C tests dependence on the fine-tuning algorithm, sentiment direction, earlier pretraining stages and substantially larger models. Figures 7–11 provide new evidence addressing these robustness and generality questions.

E5.justification: v3 Figures 5–6 newly report shaded standard deviations when combining positive-data-volume settings, replacing separately displayed curves. Neither version specifies repeated-seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests; the bands do not establish additional experimental runs.

E6.justification: Appendix C adds outcomes supporting elasticity under DPO, reversed sentiment training, earlier checkpoints and a 72B model. Table 1 retains all 54 numerical values, and v1 Figure 3's curves are retained in v3 Figure 4. The scaling plots also replace separate pretrained safety references with a common reference near -11; these display changes do not establish performance gains.

T1.justification: v3 Definition 3.1 replaces v1's whole-dataset-normalized ratio with log M minus dataset compression. Appendix B rewrites the elasticity proof accordingly, changing its reported limiting constant from alpha(alpha+1)(1-log c) to alpha squared. The leaf-node concentration assumption is omitted, and Section 3.3 adds a derivation connecting dataset size and KL-divergence changes to Hooke's law.

C1.justification: The central alignment-fragility claim remains, but v3 elevates the claim that deeper positive alignment produces faster rebound and worse performance after inverse fine-tuning. Its introduction also foregrounds a dataset-size/compression-change invariant and claims the first exploration of the proposed resistance mechanism.

C2.justification: v3 distinguishes rebound when far from the pretrained distribution from resistance near it, and develops resource-allocation and spring-based explanations. Appendix C adds interpretations concerning algorithm and sentiment-direction independence. The principal limitations remain, while broader impacts newly discuss data-cleansing costs and changes to the offence-defence balance.

D1.justification: v3 removes the project-code link and documentation of AdamW parameters, weight decay, eight A800 GPUs, decoding settings and the 52K-Alpaca preparatory fine-tuning stage. It newly specifies one SFT epoch and DPO preference-label construction. These are substantial documentation changes; omitted settings do not establish changed implementation or unavailable code.

R1.justification: v3 removes the machine-unlearning discussion and associated references, while expanding positioning around superficial alignment, robust alignment and open-model governance. Additions include Qi's shallow-safety-alignment study, Wen's RLHF study and several robustness methods. The remaining alignment-fragility discussion moves to Appendix A.

P1.justification: The title gains a compression-focused subtitle, and the main narrative is extensively rewritten into 'What', 'Why' and 'How' sections. Contributions become explicit bullets, experiments move into a dedicated section, related work moves to an appendix, and the proof exposition is substantially condensed.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main layout, colored theorem boxes and redesigned conceptual diagrams. It adds a rebound pipeline and appendix figures, simplifies Table 1's headings, redraws the retained performance plots, and merges separate scaling panels into comparative curves with shaded deviations.

improvement.justification: v3 adds useful robustness evidence and clearer organization, but removes substantial reproducibility information. Its revised normalization also creates an unresolved inconsistency: Section 2.2 says smaller compression rates are better, whereas Definition 3.1 subtracts that rate from log M yet still describes smaller normalized values as better. Because this affects the central theoretical interpretation, the empirical and presentation gains do not support a reliable net-quality judgment.
